title: Research Bias: Sort It Out, Science
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss research bias in science and why it matters amid declining public trust in experts. They walk through a "top ten" style list of biases: confirmation bias (including the N-ray episode), selection and sampling bias (including self-selection, the 1936 Literary Digest/Landon polling fiasco, survivorship bias with the WWII bomber armor story, and channeling bias), question order bias and priming, interviewer bias, recall bias, acquiescence bias, publication bias and the academic publishing industry, and file drawer bias. They cover remedies such as preregistration-style acceptance at The Lancet, randomized question order, and careful wording. The episode closes with a listener mail about the show being placed on a media bias chart.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing the death of expertise
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about a space Lord single, a Trivial Pursuit co-branded game, and listener emails. Josh frames the episode around distrust of experts and how bias in science contributes to it.

segments.title: Confirmation bias and the N-ray example
segments.summary: The hosts explain that research bias occurs in planning, during, and after studies. They describe confirmation bias using René Blondlot's N-rays, which Robert W. Wood disproved by secretly removing the crystals, and note that people across all fields are prone to it.

segments.title: Sampling bias and selection bias
segments.summary: Sampling bias is described as a non-representative sample, such as university students or online-only surveys. Self-selection bias is covered, along with the 1936 Literary Digest polling error that drew from country club rosters and car owners and wrongly predicted Alf Landon would win over Roosevelt.

segments.title: Survivorship bias and channeling bias
segments.summary: Survivorship bias is explained through business studies and the WWII bomber story, where Abraham Wald advised armoring the areas without bullet holes. Channeling bias is explained using heartburn drugs and surgery outcomes, where patient severity steers treatment groups.

segments.title: Question order bias and priming
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how question order shapes survey answers, citing the General Social Survey, where honesty was picked 66 percent of the time when listed high and 48 percent when listed low. They describe priming and ways to randomize question order.

segments.title: Interviewer bias
segments.summary: Interviewer bias is described as an interviewer's tone, wording, or knowledge of a subject's status influencing responses, such as probing smoking history more intensely. Online surveys are noted as one way to reduce it, with their own pitfalls.

segments.title: Recall bias and acquiescence bias
segments.summary: Recall bias is illustrated with a joke about Dancing with the Stars and with people underreporting unhealthy habits like eating cheese. Acquiescence bias, the tendency to agree or to be disagreeable, is covered along with wording techniques to avoid it, such as the Pew voting question example.

segments.title: Sponsor break and kid listener aside
segments.summary: A short break and banter about kids listening to the show and kids' YouTube toy videos.

segments.title: Publication bias and the academic publishing industry
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh compare academic publishing to 24-hour cable news, saying journals favor positive results. They cite a 2010 finding that social science papers were about 2.3 times more likely than physical science papers to report positive results, and note that suppressing negative trials is unethical and sometimes illegal.

segments.title: File drawer bias, Proteus effect, and The Lancet's solution
segments.summary: File drawer bias is defined as burying negative results. The hosts discuss the cost of wasted replication, the Proteus effect of initial studies failing to replicate, and The Lancet accepting papers based on study design before results are known.

segments.title: Listener mail on the media bias chart
segments.summary: Listener Nicholas Bett writes about Stuff You Should Know being placed on a Media Bias Chart as one of the fairest pieces of media, and the hosts respond with thanks. The sign-off gives the contact email.
